rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: Asad cites a well-authenticated Prophetic tradition: only conscious intentions determine judgment; Bukhari, Muslim, Tirmidhi, Abu Da'ud, Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hanbal and others transmit it.
rows.anchor: the basic, extremely well-authenticated saying of the Prophet

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: In Qur'anic ethics, action includes deliberate omission and the deliberate voicing of righteous or sinful beliefs: anything consciously intended and expressed by word or deed.
rows.anchor: comprises also a deliberate omission of actions, whether good or bad

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: A person's striving will be seen on Judgment Day, when God will make people understand all they did in life.
rows.anchor: when - as the Qur'an states in many places - God "will make you [truly] understand all that you were doing [in life]"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The ultimate limit or goal encompasses the universe's beginning and end in time and space, and is both the source from which all proceeds and the destination to which all returns.
rows.anchor: the utmost limit" or "goal", circumscribing the beginning and the end of the universe both in time and in space

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Ash-shi'ra is Sirius, a first-magnitude star in Canis Major and the brightest star in the heavens, widely worshipped in pre-Islamic Arabia.
rows.anchor: a star of the first magnitude, belonging to the constellation Canis Major. Because it is the brightest star in the heavens, it was widely worshipped in pre-Islamic Arabia

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Idiomatic rabb ash-shi'ra is a metonym for the Creator and Upholder of the universe.
rows.anchor: the phrase rabb ash-shi'ra is used as a metonym for the Creator and Upholder of the universe

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to his notes on 7:65 for 'Ad and 7:73 for Thamud.
rows.anchor: For the story of the tribe of 'Ad, see second half of note 48 on 7:65; for that of the Thamud, note 56 on 7:73.

rows.speaker: Razi
rows.claim: Razi observes that 54:1 continues 53:57's warning that the approaching Last Hour draws nearer.
rows.anchor: AS RAZI points out, the first verse of this surah appears almost like a continuation of the last verses of the preceding one, especially 53: 57

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad infers that the two surahs were revealed around the same time, late in early prophethood, perhaps in its fourth year.
rows.anchor: we may assume that both were revealed at approximately the same time, i.e., towards the end of the early part (perhaps the fourth year)

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the verse with reports from Companions that contemporaries saw the moon appear as two distinct parts one night.
rows.anchor: Most of the commentators see in this verse a reference to a phenomenon said to have been witnessed by several of the Prophet's contemporaries

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad accepts the reports' subjective sincerity but suggests an unusual partial lunar eclipse may have produced the optical illusion.
rows.anchor: no reason to doubt the subjective veracity of these reports, it is possible

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad holds that the verse does not refer to the contemporaries' reported sighting, but to a future event as the Last Hour approaches.
rows.anchor: it is practically certain that the above Qur'an-verse does not refer to it but, rather, to a future event

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses past tense for future events, especially the Hour and Resurrection, to stress that their occurrence is certain.
rows.anchor: The Qur'an frequently employs the past tense to denote the future, and particularly so in passages

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad prefers Raghib's reading of the moon's splitting as the cosmic cataclysm ending the world before Resurrection; Zamakhshari notes support for it among early commentators, and the juxtaposition with the approaching Hour convinces Asad.
rows.anchor: Raghib regards it as fully justifiable to interpret the phrase inshaqqa 'l-qamar ("the moon. is split asunder") as bearing on the cosmic cataclysm

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Qur'anic references to the Last Hour's nearness do not follow the human concept of time.
rows.anchor: none of the Qur'anic allusions to the "nearness" of the Last Hour and the Day of Resurrection is based on the human concept of "time"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Al-bayan means making something intellectually circumscribed and clear (Raghib), covering thought that distinguishes concepts and clear expression in speech or writing (Taj al-'Arus).
rows.anchor: al-bayan - denoting "the means whereby a thing is [intellectually] circumscribed and made clear" (Raghib) - applies to both thought and speech

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: In context al-bayan is articulate thought and speech, recalling man's God-given conceptual faculty, the knowledge of all names.
rows.anchor: hence, in the above context, "articulate thought and speech", recalling the "knowledge of all the names"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Sinners need not be questioned because their deeds will confront them in the record and their own tongues, hands, and feet will testify to what they did.
rows.anchor: I.e., the sinners "will find all that they ever wrought [nowl facing them" (18:49)

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Seizing sinners by forelocks and feet signifies utter humiliation; ancient Arabs used having one's forelock in another's hand as an idiom for subjection.
rows.anchor: When the ancient Arabs wanted to stress someone's subjection to another person, they would say, "His forelock is in the hand of so-and-so."

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The event that must come to pass is the Last Hour and Resurrection.
rows.anchor: I.e. the Last Hour and Resurrection

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The apostles came from among their own people, carrying divine messages specifically intended for them.
rows.anchor: apostles from their own midst, entrusted with divine messages specifically meant for them

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The phrase behind 'time and again' implies repeated visits over a duration.
rows.anchor: The expression "time and again" is conditioned by the phrase kanat ta'atihim which implies repetition and duration

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The rejecters' reply literally means 'guide us.'
rows.anchor: Lit., "guide us". This negative response is characteristic of people

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Estrangement from moral standards makes people deeply distrust human beings, so they cannot accept that divine guidance may come through ordinary people lacking supernatural qualities.
rows.anchor: their own estrangement from all moral standards, are instinctively, and deeply, distrustful of all things human

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad dates the surah to the second half of the Medina period, probably 7 AH.
rows.anchor: REVEALED in the second half of the Medina period - probably in 7 H.

rows.speaker: Zamakhshari
rows.claim: Zamakhshari records the alternate title 'Surah of the Prophet', since its first half concerns aspects of Muhammad's personal and family life.
rows.anchor: occasionally designated as "The Surah of the Prophet" (Zamakhshari) inasmuch as the first half

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Ahl literally means family or people, but can include people sharing race, religion, or occupation, and dependants in the broadest sense.
rows.anchor: the term ahl denotes also people who share one's race, religion, occupation, etc., as well as "dependants"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad refers to his explanation of the fire's fuel at 2:24.
rows.anchor: See surah 2, note 16.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to his allegorical explanation of the passage about Hell's keepers at 74:27 and following.
rows.anchor: See 74:27 ff. and the corresponding notes, particularly notes 15 and 16

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The angels are subject to God's law of cause and effect, which governs the spiritual realm as it does the material world.
rows.anchor: these angelic powers are subject to the God-willed law of cause and effect which dominates the realm of the spirit no less than the world of matter

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: This is chronologically the first occurrence of the disjointed letters that precede some Qur'anic surahs; Asad points to Appendix II for theories about them.
rows.anchor: Chronologically, this is the first appearance of any of the "disjointed" [i.e., single] letters

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Some early commentators cited by Tabari take nun as an abbreviation for a homonymous noun meaning great fish or inkwell; Asad rejects this on the grammatical grounds advanced by Zamakhshari and Razi.
rows.anchor: the letter n, pronounced nun, represents here an abbreviation of the identically-pronounced noun which signifies both "great fish" and "inkwell"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad points to 74:32, note 23, for the meaning of the oath particle wa.
rows.anchor: For the meaning of the adjurative particle wa at the beginning of this sentence, see first half of note 23 on 74:32.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The pen recalls the first revelation, 96:1-5, and thereby emphasizes Muhammad's prophethood.
rows.anchor: The mention of "the pen" is meant to recall the earliest Qur'anic revelation, namely, the first five verses of surah 96

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: For the pen's symbolic significance, Asad directs readers to 96:3-5 and note 3.
rows.anchor: As regards the symbolic significance of the concept of "the pen", see 96:3-5 and the corresponding note 3.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The claim that Muhammad was mad recalls the taunt used by most contemporaries from the start of his preaching and continued for years.
rows.anchor: This is an allusion to the taunt with which most of Muhammad's contemporaries greeted the beginning of his preaching

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: More broadly, the passage applies to all followers who base moral judgments on belief in God and the afterlife.
rows.anchor: not merely to the Prophet but also to all who followed or will follow him: in this particular instance, to all who base their moral valuations on their belief in God and in life after death

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Khuluq can mean character, innate disposition or nature, as well as habitual behavior that becomes second nature (Taj al-'Arus).
rows.anchor: The term khuluq, rendered by me as "way of life", describes a person's "character", "innate disposition" or "nature"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad renders khuluq as 'way of life', following Ibn Abbas's equation with din and the latter's primary sense of a way or manner of acting.
rows.anchor: explanation of the above verse by Abd Allah ibn Abbas (as quoted by Tabari), stating that this term is here synonymous with din

rows.speaker: A'ishah
rows.claim: In well-authenticated traditions, A'ishah repeatedly said of Muhammad that his way of life was the Qur'an; Asad lists reports transmitted through several authorities and compilations.
rows.anchor: his way of life (khuluq) was the Qur'an." (Muslim, Tabari and Hakim, on the authority of Said ibn Hisham

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The opponents want ethical and moral concessions from the Prophet, promising to reciprocate and stop actively opposing him.
rows.anchor: they would like thee to be conciliatory in the matter of ethical principles and moral valuations, whereupon they would reciprocate and desist from actively opposing thee

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The image of the shin being bared means that people's innermost thoughts, feelings, and motivations will be exposed.
rows.anchor: when man's innermost thoughts, feelings and motivations will be laid bare

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: This exposure lays bare as indefensible and spiritually destructive the former claim that whatever is expedient is morally justifiable.
rows.anchor: their erstwhile claim that whatever is "expedient" is morally justifiable (see note 19 above), shall be revealed in all its nakedness - namely, as something indefensible and spiritually destructive

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The call to prostrate means willingly and gladly humbling oneself before God.
rows.anchor: I.e., willingly, gladly humbling themselves before Him

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Asad directs readers to compare the destruction of Thamud with 7:78.

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The overthrown cities are Sodom and Gomorrah, the cities of Lot's people.
rows.anchor: Sodom and Gomorrah, the cities of Lot's people

rows.speaker: classical commentators
rows.claim: In the consensus of classical commentators, 'you' refers metonymically to your ancestors.
rows.anchor: metonymically (in the consensus of all classical commentators), "your ancestors"

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: The reminder points both to evildoers' punishment and to the saving grace bestowed on the righteous.
rows.anchor: Alluding to the punishment of evildoers and the saving grace bestowed upon the righteous

rows.speaker: Asad
rows.claim: Receiving the record in the left hand signifies an unrighteous earthly life, in contrast with receiving it in the right hand.
rows.anchor: signifying that he had been unrighteous in his earthly life, in contrast with those "whose record will be placed in their right hand"

rows.speaker: Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak
rows.claim: These exegetes, quoted by Tabari, take sultan as argument or hujjah; Asad adopts this sense for arguments against life after death and divine judgment, though the word primarily means power or authority.
rows.anchor: meaning of "argument", synonymous with hujjah (Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Ad-Dahhak, all of them quoted by Tabari)
